brief.title: From Shakespeare text to integer ids
brief.objective: Follow how prepare.py turns raw text into integer ids. It collects the sorted unique characters as the vocabulary, gives each character its index in that list, splits the text 90/10 by position, and then encodes each split one character at a time.
brief.audience_context: The learner pointed at lines 23-45 of data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py in nanoGPT, the character-level data preparation step, and asked for a 15-second explanation. No earlier concept or lesson is recorded.
brief.scope_note: To fit 15 seconds, the video leaves out the print statements and treats decode/itos as optional, at most a brief reverse arrow. It also skips anything outside lines 23-45, such as downloading the text and saving the ids to files.

evidence.excerpt:
# get all the unique characters that occur in this text
chars = sorted(list(set(data)))
vocab_size = len(chars)
print("all the unique characters:", ''.join(chars))
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size:,}")

# create a mapping from characters to integers
stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }
itos = { i:ch for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[c] for c in s] # encoder: take a string, output a list of integers
def decode(l):
    return ''.join([itos[i] for i in l]) # decoder: take a list of integers, output a string

# create the train and test splits
n = len(data)
train_data = data[:int(n*0.9)]
val_data = data[int(n*0.9):]

# encode both to integers
train_ids = encode(train_data)
val_ids = encode(val_data)
print(f"train has {len(train_ids):,} tokens")

claim_registry.text: chars = sorted(list(set(data))) collects every unique character in the whole text, in sorted order, and vocab_size = len(chars) is the number of those characters.
stoi maps each character to its index in chars (via enumerate(chars)), and encode(s) returns [stoi[c] for c in s]: one integer per character of the string.
itos is the reverse mapping from index to character, and decode(l) joins the looked-up characters back into a string.
The text is split by position: train_data = data[:int(n*0.9)] is the first 90% and val_data = data[int(n*0.9):] is the remaining 10%.
After the split, both parts go through encode, which produces train_ids and val_ids.

must_show: A short sample of raw text collapsing into a sorted row of unique characters (chars), with its length labelled vocab_size
Each character in that sorted row tagged with its index number, labelled stoi
A short string passing through encode and coming out as a list of integers, one per character, each looked up from the stoi row
The full text bar cut at the 90% mark into a front train_data part and a back val_data part
Both parts then passing through encode to become train_ids and val_ids
must_not_claim: That the integer ids are ASCII or Unicode code points (they are positions in the sorted chars list)
That set(data) alone gives a fixed order (the order comes from sorted)
That the vocabulary is built from the training split only (it is built from the whole text before splitting)
That the train/val split is random or shuffled (it is a contiguous cut: first 90% and last 10%)
That encoding happens before splitting (the code splits first, then encodes each part)
That tokens are words or subwords, or that encode merges characters (each character becomes exactly one integer)
That encode compresses or changes the content of the text (it is a reversible lookup; decode recovers the string)
brief.visual_direction: Let the viewer's eye move left to right through one pipeline. First the raw text breaks into characters, duplicates merge, and the survivors line up in sorted order. A number appears under each one, and that numbered row stays on screen as the lookup table. Next a short word slides under the table and each letter drops its matching number, so the viewer sees a one-character-to-one-integer swap. Then pull back to the whole text as one long bar. Cut it at the 90% mark without shuffling, then send each piece through the same lookup so it comes out as a stream of integers. Keep the lookup table visible the whole time, so the viewer can tell that one shared vocabulary encodes both splits.
